subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage:
"No!" Parveen marched across the room holding up the toy car, which had gone quiet.
"What happened?" asked Yogesh, Parveen's father, taking it.
"No," Parveen said again, tapping the car.
"No more noise? Let me look." Yogesh slid the battery cover open and pressed the battery back in. The car whirred.
"Vroom!" said Parveen, and grabbed it back.

qa.q: What did Parveen carry across the room?
qa.a: Parveen carried the toy car, which had gone quiet.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when tapping the silent car?
qa.a: Parveen was upset and expectant, wanting the noise back and sure Yogesh would fix it.

qa.q: What could Parveen try before bringing the car over, and why?
qa.a: Parveen could press the button or shake it once first, because a small try might work, and asking would still be available.

qa.q: How does the request look to Yogesh?
qa.a: Yogesh sees the short "No" as a clear cry for help, and he finds the fault quickly, so being asked works well for him.

grounding: A toddler carries a silent toy car to the father, holds it up and says "no," treating the father as the repair service.

passage:
Rekha's shoe strap flapped loose in the hallway. Rekha stared at it, then shouted toward the next room, "Dadi! Dadi!"
Dadi came out drying her hands. "What broke?"
"Mummy said Dadi," Rekha announced, pointing at the shoe. "Dadi fix."
Farida, Rekha's mother, laughed from the stairs. "I do shout that a lot, don't I?"
Dadi crouched and pressed the strap down.

qa.q: What did Rekha shout toward the next room?
qa.a: Rekha shouted "Dadi! Dadi!" toward the next room.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when announcing "Dadi fix"?
qa.a: Rekha was pleased and sure of the plan, and the announcement shows Rekha thought calling for Dadi is the way to get things fixed.

qa.q: What could Rekha do next time if Dadi does not hear, and why?
qa.a: Rekha could carry the shoe to Dadi or go find Dadi, because moving closer helps when a shout does not carry.

qa.q: How does Farida see Rekha's copying?
qa.a: Farida is amused and a little embarrassed to hear her own habit repeated, as her laugh and "I do shout that a lot" show.

grounding: A toddler who has heard mother call "Dadi!" when something breaks shouts "Dadi" toward the next room when a shoe strap comes loose.

passage: On the charpai in the courtyard Zeenat shook the silent toy, then banged it on the floor, then pressed its button again and again. Nothing. Only then did Zeenat slide down and toddle toward the kitchen, holding it out in front. Rekha, Zeenat's mother, was stirring dal at the chulha. She wiped her hands, pressed the battery lid, and the toy sang again.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do before setting off for the kitchen?
qa.a: Zeenat shook the silent toy, banged it on the floor and pressed its button again and again.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling as the toy stayed silent?
qa.a: Zeenat was frustrated and puzzled, which is why Zeenat gave up trying alone and went to find Rekha.

qa.q: What alternative could Zeenat use if shaking and pressing fail again, and why?
qa.a: Zeenat could go to Rekha sooner, or bring the toy along while calling out, because asking early saves the effort when nothing else works. 🙂

qa.q: How might Rekha see the toy being brought to her?
qa.a: Rekha sees a toddler who tried first and now wants help, so the quick fix at the battery lid is easy for Rekha and pleasing for Zeenat.

grounding: A toddler shakes, bangs and presses a silent toy on their own first, and only when nothing works goes to find mother.

passage: Nursery note, Monday. From the kitchen I heard Karthik screaming and hurried in, expecting an injury. Karthik stood rooted by the sofa, red-faced, waiting for someone to come. I checked hands, feet and head. Nothing seemed wrong, but the screaming went on and I could not tell what the problem was. Only when I knelt down did I see a teddy ear behind the sofa. I lifted the teddy out. Next time I will teach Karthik to point. Kunal

qa.q: Where did Karthik stand while screaming?
qa.a: Karthik stood by the sofa.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling while waiting by the sofa?
qa.a: Karthik was angry and desperate to be helped, screaming in place and hoping someone would come.

qa.q: What could Karthik try in place of screaming from one spot, and why?
qa.a: Karthik could walk to Kunal and point at the sofa, because showing the problem tells an adult what is wrong much faster than noise alone.

qa.q: How does Kunal see the screaming?
qa.a: Kunal hears loud distress but cannot tell what is wrong, so Kunal fears an injury at first and searches until the teddy ear appears.

grounding: A toddler with a teddy wedged behind the sofa screams from one spot and waits, so the caregiver cannot tell what is wrong and help is late.

subtype: Approach: leading the caregiver by hand [Revision]
passage:
"Tedi! Tedi!" Zeynep cried from the living room. Dalia, Zeynep's mother, was drying dishes. "One minute, Zeynep!"
The calling stopped. Zeynep marched into the kitchen, seized Dalia's finger and pulled toward the sofa, the other hand jabbing at the gap. "Oh, teddy fell behind?" Dalia knelt down, reached in and fished it out. Zeynep hugged it, then patted Dalia's cheek.

qa.q: What did Zeynep grab to pull Dalia to the sofa?
qa.a: Zeynep seized Dalia's finger and pulled toward the sofa.

qa.q: What was Zeynep feeling when Dalia said "One minute"?
qa.a: Zeynep was impatient and worried about the teddy, but stayed determined and found another way to make Dalia understand.

qa.q: What other approach could Zeynep use next time, and why?
qa.a: Zeynep could point and say "stuck" while walking over, because words plus pointing might help Dalia understand even faster.

qa.q: How does Dalia see the finger-pulling?
qa.a: Dalia was busy and did not know what was wrong, but the pull and the pointing showed her clearly, so she came and fixed it.

grounding: When mother says "wait a minute," a toddler grabs her finger and leads her to the sofa, pointing at the teddy, which fixes the missing message.

passage: Nursery note, Tuesday. From the doorway I saw Mahima push an arm into the gap behind the sofa, tug at the teddy and fail. Mahima stopped, looked at the gap and walked off to the blocks without a word to anyone. The teddy stayed behind the sofa until I found it much later. At nap time Mahima asked for it and cried when it was not there. I found it and we talked about pointing and saying "stuck." Mehak

qa.q: Where did Mahima walk off to?
qa.a: Mahima walked off to the blocks.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling at nap time when the teddy was not there?
qa.a: Mahima was sad and missed the teddy, and the crying shows the loss had not been forgotten.

qa.q: What could Mahima try instead of walking away, and why?
qa.a: Mahima could tell Mehak or point at the gap, because an adult can reach the teddy and solve the problem quickly.

qa.q: How does Mehak see the missing teddy?
qa.a: Mehak saw the failed try but was not told, so the teddy was lost until nap time, and Mehak wants Mahima to learn to ask.

grounding: A toddler stops trying to free a wedged teddy, walks away and tells no one, so the toy stays lost until a caregiver finds it later.

subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage: I was visiting when Dolma brought an empty katori to Himani, Dolma's mother, and tapped its rim, saying "aur." The word was small and unclear, but the bowl was held right under Himani's nose. Himani smiled, took it and filled it again with dal-rice. I doubt Dolma could have said much more, and the bowl did the talking. I can only guess at Dolma's feelings. Hungry, certainly. A neighbour

qa.q: What did Dolma bring to Himani?
qa.a: Dolma brought an empty katori to Himani.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling, and how sure is the neighbour?
qa.a: Dolma was probably hungry and hopeful, but the neighbour says only that hunger is certain and the rest is a guess from the tapping and the held-out bowl.

qa.q: What other approach could Dolma use, and why?
qa.a: Dolma could add a word like "dal" to say what is wanted, because a clearer word helps an adult choose the right food. 😊

qa.q: How does Himani see the tapping of the bowl?
qa.a: Himani sees an empty bowl and an unclear word as a clear request, so she smiles and fills it, which shows the bowl is enough of a message for her.

grounding: A toddler brings an empty katori to mother and taps it, saying "aur," so that handing over the bowl says more than the word.

passage: Tanvir toddled into the flat's kitchen and tugged at the cupboard where the biscuits lived. It stayed shut. Next Tanvir gripped the fridge handle and pulled with both hands. The door did not budge. Then Tanvir looked up at the counter, pointed and grunted. Yash, Tanvir's father, looked up from his laptop. "Biscuit? Come." Tanvir walked over, hands lifted.

qa.q: What did Tanvir grip after the cupboard stayed shut?
qa.a: Tanvir gripped the fridge handle and pulled with both hands.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when pointing and grunting at the counter?
qa.a: Tanvir was hungry and hopeful, and the pointing shows a wish to get what the earlier tries could not reach.

qa.q: What alternative could Tanvir use sooner, and why?
qa.a: Tanvir could go straight to Yash and point at the cupboard, because tugging at doors that stay shut only takes time when an adult can help.

qa.q: How does Yash see Tanvir's tries?
qa.a: Yash sees a hungry child working through the reachable options and then pointing, so he answers with a friendly "Biscuit? Come."

grounding: A toddler tugs at the kitchen cupboard, then at the fridge handle, then points at the counter, learning what can be reached.

passage:
"Roti, please," said Jaya, Jagdish's mother, passing the plate to Papa.
"Roti," said Papa.
"Roti!" Jagdish held out both hands. "Roti, roti. Like Mummy."
Jaya laughed. "You said it just like we do."
"Roti," Jagdish said again, hands still open.
Papa tore off a small piece. "Here you go. Say thank you."
"Tank oo," said Jagdish, and chewed happily.

qa.q: What word did Jagdish say with both hands held out?
qa.a: Jagdish said "Roti!" with both hands held out.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling after saying "Roti" like Mummy?
qa.a: Jagdish was eager and pleased, feeling that the word could make food appear.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish try if the word is not heard at a noisy meal, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish could touch Papa's arm or point at the roti while saying it, because a gesture plus a word is easier to notice.

qa.q: How does Jaya see Jagdish copying the family's word?
qa.a: Jaya is amused and touched to hear the family's own word repeated, as her laugh and "You said it just like we do" show.

grounding: At mealtime a toddler copies the family, saying "roti" and holding out both hands, treating a learned word as a way to make food appear.

passage: Nursery note, Thursday. At the sandpit Tenzin rubbed a belly and said "num," with nobody near, then looked around. Tenzin's grandmother told me that this began when the same tummy rub and "num" once brought a cup of milk at home. Since then Tenzin rubs and says it whenever hungry, whether anyone is watching or not. I said, "Snack soon," and Tenzin nodded. I will try teaching a word to pair with it. Sabina

qa.q: Where was Tenzin when rubbing the belly and saying "num"?
qa.a: Tenzin was at the sandpit.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's repeated rubbing suggest Tenzin is feeling?
qa.a: Tenzin is hungry and confident that the rub and "num" work, since repeating them worked before with milk.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do if nobody is looking, and why?
qa.a: Tenzin could go to Sabina and say "num" or point at the snack shelf, because a signal only works when someone sees or hears it.

qa.q: How does Tenzin's grandmother see the belly rub?
qa.a: Tenzin's grandmother remembers it as the moment the plan began, when it brought milk, so it probably feels like a family story and a sign Tenzin learns from what works.

grounding: A toddler who once got milk by rubbing the tummy and saying "num" now rubs the belly whenever hungry, whether or not anyone is looking.
